topics.title: Composition and vertical structure (troposphere to thermosphere)
lesson: Dry air is about 78.08% nitrogen, 20.95% oxygen and 0.93% argon. Carbon dioxide is only about 0.04%. Water vapour is the variable gas (up to about 4% by volume) and it drives most weather. Ozone is a trace gas but it controls the temperature structure of the stratosphere.

lesson.h: The layers, from the ground up

list: Troposphere: surface to the tropopause. Temperature falls with height (average about 6.5 C per km). Holds about 75% of the atmosphere's mass (SKYbrary) and roughly 99% of its water vapour (UCAR), so nearly all weather occurs here.

Stratosphere: tropopause to about 50 km. Temperature rises with height because of heat released as ozone forms and absorbs ultraviolet radiation. Contains the ozone layer, which absorbs ultraviolet light and converts it to heat (UCAR). Very stable, little vertical mixing, almost no weather.
Mesosphere: to about 85 km. Temperature falls again. The coldest temperatures in the atmosphere, about -90 C, are found near its top (UCAR), at the mesopause.

Thermosphere: above about 85 km. Temperature rises sharply. The ionosphere is not a separate layer: it is a series of regions in parts of the mesosphere and thermosphere where solar radiation produces ions (UCAR).

lesson: The boundaries are named after the layer below them: tropopause, stratopause, mesopause. The tropopause height varies with latitude. NOAA gives about 6 km at the poles, about 9 km near 50 degrees latitude and 18 to 20 km at the equator. The ISA uses a single value of 11 km.

lesson.note: Why it matters: jet streams and the strongest turbulence sit near the tropopause, and thunderstorm tops are capped by it.

terms: Tropopause
Boundary between the troposphere and stratosphere, where temperature stops decreasing with height.
Ozone layer
Region of the stratosphere where most atmospheric ozone sits. Ozone formation and UV absorption warm the stratosphere.
Environmental lapse rate
The actual rate at which temperature changes with height at a given place and time.

questions.q: Which layer of the atmosphere contains nearly all weather?
questions.e: The troposphere holds most of the atmosphere's mass and nearly all of its water vapour, so nearly all weather occurs there.

questions.q: Why does temperature increase with height in the stratosphere?
c: The ground radiates more heat at that height
questions.e: NOAA: the stratosphere warms with height because heat is released when ozone forms. Ozone absorbs ultraviolet radiation.

questions.q: Where is the tropopause typically highest?
c: It is the same height everywhere
questions.e: NOAA: the tropopause is about 18 to 20 km at the equator, about 9 km at 50 degrees latitude and about 6 km at the poles.

questions.q: What is the most abundant gas in dry air?
questions.e: Nitrogen makes up about 78% of dry air, oxygen about 21%.

questions.q: In which layer does temperature decrease with height AND most mass of the atmosphere reside?
questions.e: The troposphere has falling temperature with height and holds about 75% of the atmosphere's mass.

questions.q: About what fraction of the atmosphere's mass lies in the troposphere?
questions.e: The troposphere holds about 75% of the atmosphere's mass (SKYbrary).

questions.q: According to NOAA, about how high does the stratosphere extend?
questions.e: NOAA: the stratosphere reaches to about 50 km (31 miles). The mesosphere runs to about 85 km and the thermosphere to about 600 km.

questions.q: In which layer is most atmospheric ozone found?
c: In the troposphere just above the ground
questions.e: The ozone layer sits in the stratosphere. The 15 to 35 km range was not confirmed and was removed.

questions.q: Which atmospheric gas varies most in concentration and drives most weather?
questions.e: Water vapour ranges from near zero to about 4% and its phase changes release or absorb latent heat.

questions.q: What tropopause height does the International Standard Atmosphere use?
questions.e: ISA places the tropopause at 11 km, where the temperature is -56.5 C.

questions.q: What happens to temperature just above the tropopause?
c: It stays nearly constant, then increases with height
It rises sharply at once, by about 30 C in the first kilometre
It keeps falling at the same 6.5 C per km rate as below
It drops steadily toward the coldest values of the mesopause
questions.e: In the ISA the temperature is constant at -56.5 C from 11 to 20 km.

questions.q: According to NOAA, about how high is the tropopause at the poles?
questions.e: NOAA: about 6 km at the poles, about 9 km near 50 degrees latitude and 18 to 20 km at the equator.

sources: NOAA JetStream, Composition of the atmosphere: gas percentages and water vapour up to about 4%
NOAA JetStream, Layers of the atmosphere: layer boundaries, temperature trends, tropopause height by latitude, stratosphere share of gases
ISO 2533:1975 / ICAO Doc 7488 (via the International Standard Atmosphere article): 11 km tropopause

UCAR SciEd, Layers of the atmosphere: layer tops, ozone in stratosphere, coldest temperatures (about -90 C) near top of mesosphere, ionosphere in parts of mesosphere and thermosphere, 99% of water vapour in troposphere
SKYbrary, Troposphere: 75% of atmospheric mass, tropopause about 11 km
WCIA Weather 101, Layers of the atmosphere (TV station, secondary): 75% of atmospheric mass in the troposphere (agrees with SKYbrary)
unverified: Mesopause named explicitly as the coldest region: UCAR says coldest temperatures are near the top of the mesosphere (same place). Lesson now says so.
The earlier claim that the tropopause is lower in winter was removed (not confirmed).

topics.title: Temperature, pressure, humidity relationships
lesson: Three variables describe the state of the air: temperature, pressure and humidity. They are tied together, and most forecasting reasoning starts here.
Pressure at a point is the weight of the column of air above it. It always decreases with height, fastest near the surface. Pressure is measured in hectopascals (hPa), where 1 hPa equals 1 millibar.

lesson.h: Temperature, density and the gas law

lesson.formula:
p = rho * R * T
(p = pressure, rho = density, R = 287 J/kg/K for dry air, T in kelvin)

lesson: At the same pressure, warmer air is less dense, so it tends to rise. Cold air is denser and sinks. This is the basis of convection and of the sea breeze.

list: Warm air can hold much more water vapour than cold air. The saturation vapour pressure rises about 7% for each 1 C of warming (Penn State METEO 300).
Relative humidity (RH) is how close the air is to saturation. Cool the air at constant moisture and RH rises.
Dew point is the temperature the air must be cooled to (at constant pressure and moisture) to reach saturation. Dew point only changes when moisture is added or removed.
When temperature equals dew point, RH is 100%. A small temperature-dew point spread means cloud or fog is close.

lesson.note: Shortcut: a spread of 0 to 2 C with light winds and clear skies at night is a standard fog warning sign.

terms: hPa
Hectopascal, the standard unit of pressure. Equal to one millibar.
Relative humidity
Ratio of actual vapour pressure to saturation vapour pressure, as a percentage.
Dew point
Temperature at which air becomes saturated when cooled at constant pressure and moisture.
Spread
Temperature minus dew point. Small spread means near saturation.

questions.q: Air is cooled at constant pressure with no moisture added or removed. What happens to its relative humidity?
questions.e: Cooler air can hold less water vapour, so the same vapour content is a larger fraction of saturation and RH rises.

questions.q: What is the dew point?
c: The temperature to which air must be cooled, at constant pressure and moisture, to become saturated
The temperature at which water in the air first freezes, found by cooling at constant volume
The temperature at which relative humidity falls to 50% when pressure is held constant
The lowest air temperature recorded overnight once extra moisture has been added to the air
questions.e: Dew point is defined by cooling at constant pressure and moisture content until saturation is reached.

questions.q: At the same pressure, how does warm air compare with cold air?
questions.e: From the gas law p = rho R T, at constant p a higher T means lower density.

questions.q: On a calm, clear night the temperature is 4 C and the dew point is 3 C. What is the most likely development?
questions.e: A 1 C spread means the air is nearly saturated. With continued radiational cooling, fog is likely.

questions.q: What does the pressure at a point on the ground represent?
c: The weight of the air column above it
The temperature of the air above it
The speed of the wind at that point
The humidity of the air above it
questions.e: Atmospheric pressure is the weight of the overlying column of air per unit area.

questions.q: Air at 18 C has a dew point of 15 C. What is the temperature-dew point spread?
questions.e: Spread = temperature minus dew point = 18 - 15 = 3 C.

questions.q: Air at 25 C has a dew point of 25 C. What is its relative humidity?
questions.e: When temperature equals dew point the air is saturated.

questions.q: Station pressure falls steadily for several hours as cloud thickens and the wind backs. What is most likely approaching?
c: A low-pressure system or warm front
Building high pressure with clearing skies
A stationary ridge with light winds
A sea breeze from the north
questions.e: Falling pressure with thickening cloud and backing wind is the classic sign of an approaching low or warm front.

questions.q: Which relation links pressure, density and temperature of air?
questions.e: The ideal gas law, p = rho R T, ties the three variables together.

questions.q: A pressure of 1000 hPa equals how many kilopascals?
Moist air is cooled until its temperature reaches the dew point. What happens next?
c: Condensation begins as cloud, fog or dew
The dew point rises above the air temperature
questions.e: At the dew point the air is saturated, and further cooling forces vapour to condense.

questions.q: By about how much does saturation vapour pressure rise for each 1 C of warming?
questions.e: Penn State METEO 300: saturation vapour pressure increases by about 7% for every 1 K (1 C).

sources: Penn State METEO 300, Fundamentals of Atmospheric Science: saturation vapour pressure rises about 7% per 1 K; dew point definition and dew point never above air temperature
unverified: Relative humidity definition, ideal gas law with R = 287 J/kg/K, hPa = mbar: standard physics, not checked on a Canadian publication.
Fog warning at a spread of 0 to 2 C, and falling pressure with backing wind as a sign of an approaching low or warm front: operational rules of thumb, not confirmed.
Source is a university course text, not a Canadian government publication.

topics.title: Hydrostatic balance and the standard atmosphere
lesson: On large scales the atmosphere is in hydrostatic balance: the upward pressure gradient force balances gravity. Pressure drops with height at a rate set by air density.

Because cold air is denser, pressure falls faster with height in cold air. The layer between two pressure levels is therefore thinner when cold and thicker when warm. This is the hypsometric relationship, and it is why thickness charts work as temperature charts.

list: 1000-500 hPa thickness near 540 dam (5,400 m) is used as a rough rain/snow line and roughly divides polar from mid-latitude air (NOAA NWS). Other sources put the equal-chance value nearer 522 dam, and the deep layer is a weak snow indicator. The 850-1000 hPa thickness is used for snow probability. Use it as a guide only.
Near sea level, pressure falls about 1 hPa for every 8 m (about 27 ft) of height. This follows from the hydrostatic equation with ISA sea-level density: 100 Pa / (1.225 x 9.81) = 8.3 m.
Sea level: 1013.25 hPa (101,325 Pa) and 15 C. Defined in ISO 2533:1975 and ICAO Doc 7488.
Temperature falls 6.5 C per km (about 2 C per 1,000 ft) up to 11 km, where it is -56.5 C.
Above 11 km it is isothermal at -56.5 C up to 20 km.

lesson.h: Approximate heights of standard pressure levels

list: 850 hPa: about 1,460 m (4,800 ft)
700 hPa: about 3,010 m (9,900 ft)

250 hPa: about 10,360 m (34,000 ft). Charts label these levels 5,000, 10,000, 18,000 and 34,000 ft. Heights above are the standard-atmosphere values in a public meteorology training table (heights to the nearest foot: 850 hPa 4,781; 700 hPa 9,882; 500 hPa 18,289; 300 hPa 30,065; 250 hPa 33,999).

lesson.note: Real heights vary with the actual temperature. A 500 hPa height of 5,100 m means a cold column; 5,800 m means a warm one.

terms: Hydrostatic balance
Balance between the vertical pressure gradient force and gravity.
Thickness
Vertical distance between two pressure levels. Proportional to mean layer temperature.
ISA
International Standard Atmosphere: a reference profile starting at 15 C and 1013.25 hPa.

questions.q: What are the ISA sea-level temperature and pressure?
questions.e: ISA is defined as 15 C and 1013.25 hPa at mean sea level.

questions.q: What does a warmer layer do to the thickness between two pressure levels?
questions.e: Warm air is less dense, so a greater depth is needed to span the same pressure difference.

questions.q: What is the ISA lapse rate in the troposphere?
questions.e: ISA uses 6.5 C/km (about 2 C per 1,000 ft) up to 11 km.

questions.q: What does hydrostatic balance mean?
c: The vertical pressure gradient force balances gravity
Horizontal pressure and Coriolis forces balance
Pressure is the same at all heights
questions.e: In hydrostatic balance the upward pressure gradient force equals the downward force of gravity.

questions.q: About how high is the 500 hPa level in the standard atmosphere?
questions.e: 500 hPa sits near 5,570 m in the ISA (computed from the ISA equations), which is why it is treated as the mid-troposphere level.

questions.q: What is the ISA temperature at 11 km?
questions.e: ISA falls 6.5 C per km from 15 C to -56.5 C at 11 km, then stays constant to 20 km.

questions.q: Using the ISA lapse rate of 6.5 C per km, what is the ISA temperature at 3,000 m?
About how high is the 850 hPa level in the standard atmosphere?
questions.e: 850 hPa is near 1,460 m in the ISA, a good proxy for low-level temperature and moisture.

questions.q: Which pressure level sits near 10,400 m (about flight level 340)?
questions.e: 250 hPa is near 10,360 m (about 34,000 ft) in the ISA and is a standard jet stream level.

questions.q: A 1000-500 hPa thickness of 5,100 m compared with 5,700 m indicates the 5,100 m layer is:
c: More stable but the same temperature
questions.e: Thickness is proportional to the mean temperature of the layer.

questions.q: Near sea level, about how much does pressure fall for each 8 m of height gained?
questions.e: Near sea level pressure falls about 1 hPa per 8 m (about 27 ft), from the hydrostatic equation with ISA density.

sources: ISO 2533:1975 and ICAO Doc 7488 (International Standard Atmosphere): sea level 15 C and 101,325 Pa, 6.5 C per km, 11 km at -56.5 C, isothermal 11 to 20 km
NOAA NWS Houston training page on thickness (Haby): 540 dam and rain/snow, caveats
Pressure-level heights and 1 hPa per 8 m: computed here from the ISA equations
NAV CANADA Aviation Weather Services Guide (2017): 5,000, 10,000, 18,000, 34,000 ft chart labels
Navy meteorology training table (tpub.com), standard atmosphere heights: 850 hPa 1,457 m; 700 hPa 3,012 m; 500 hPa 5,574 m; 300 hPa 9,164 m; 250 hPa 10,363 m
unverified: Hydrostatic equation and hypsometric relationship: standard physics, not checked on a Canadian publication.
Warm/cold column heights at 500 hPa (5,100 m and 5,800 m): rough illustration.
300 hPa at 30,065 ft is now sourced to a US Navy training table via fetch summary. Whether Canadian charts label 300 hPa as FL300 or 30,000 ft was not confirmed.

topics.title: Stability and lapse rates (dry, moist, environmental)
lesson: Stability describes whether a displaced parcel of air returns to its starting level or keeps moving. A parcel that is warmer (less dense) than its surroundings rises. A parcel that is cooler sinks.

list: Dry adiabatic lapse rate (DALR): 9.8 C per km (about 3 C per 1,000 ft). A rising unsaturated parcel cools at this rate.

Saturated (moist) adiabatic lapse rate (SALR): less than the DALR. A typical value is around 5 C per km, with a range of about 3.6 to 9.2 C per km quoted from ICAO. It varies strongly with temperature. Condensation releases latent heat, which offsets some of the cooling. In very warm, humid air it is only about 4 to 5 C per km. In cold air it approaches the dry rate, and the wet and dry adiabats are nearly parallel in the upper troposphere (Haby).
Environmental lapse rate (ELR): the actual temperature change with height, measured by soundings. This is the one that varies day to day.
ELR less than SALR: absolutely stable.
ELR greater than DALR: absolutely unstable.
ELR between SALR and DALR: conditionally unstable. Stable while unsaturated, unstable once saturated and lifted.

lesson: An inversion (temperature increasing with height) is very stable. It acts as a lid, trapping moisture, smoke and haze below it.

list: Stable air: layered (stratiform) cloud, steady precipitation, poor visibility, smooth flight, fog and smoke trapped.
Unstable air: heaped (cumuliform) cloud, showers, good visibility outside showers, turbulence.

terms: Parcel method
Compare a lifted parcel's temperature with its surroundings to judge stability.
Inversion
A layer where temperature increases with height.
Conditional instability
Stable for unsaturated lift, unstable for saturated lift.

questions.q: What is the dry adiabatic lapse rate?
questions.e: The DALR is about 9.8 C/km (about 3 C per 1,000 ft).

questions.q: The environmental lapse rate is 12 C per km. What is the atmosphere's stability?
questions.e: An ELR greater than the DALR (9.8 C/km) means a lifted parcel is always warmer than its surroundings: absolutely unstable.

questions.q: Why is the saturated adiabatic lapse rate smaller than the dry rate?
c: Latent heat released by condensation offsets part of the cooling
Saturated air is denser, so it expands less and cools more slowly
Water vapour absorbs outgoing radiation and warms the rising parcel
Pressure falls more slowly with height inside a cloud than outside it
questions.e: Condensation releases latent heat into the parcel, so it cools more slowly than a dry parcel.

questions.q: Which weather is most typical of a stable air mass?
c: Layered cloud, poor visibility, steady precipitation
Towering cumulus, excellent visibility, scattered showers
Cumulonimbus, gusty winds, thunderstorms with hail
Cloud-free skies, strong turbulence, unlimited visibility
questions.e: Stable air resists vertical motion, so cloud forms in layers and haze or fog is trapped near the surface.

questions.q: When is the atmosphere conditionally unstable?
c: ELR is between the saturated and dry adiabatic lapse rates
ELR is smaller than the saturated adiabatic lapse rate at all levels
ELR is larger than the dry adiabatic lapse rate throughout the layer
A strong surface inversion caps the layer and traps moisture below
questions.e: Between the SALR and DALR, an unsaturated parcel is stable but a saturated one is unstable.

questions.q: A parcel at 20 C is lifted 1,000 m dry adiabatically. What is its temperature?
questions.e: Dry adiabatic cooling is 9.8 C per km, so 20 - 9.8 = about 10 C.

questions.q: Temperature is 15 C at the surface and 18 C at 500 m. What does this layer represent?
questions.e: Temperature increasing with height is an inversion.

questions.q: Which type of layer is the most stable?
c: A layer where ELR exceeds the DALR
A super-adiabatic layer over hot ground
questions.e: An inversion strongly resists any vertical motion.

questions.q: A parcel is displaced upward in a stable atmosphere. What does it do?
c: It is cooler than its surroundings and sinks back
It is warmer than its surroundings and keeps rising
It stays at the new level
It warms by compression and accelerates
questions.e: In stable air an upward-displaced parcel is denser than the environment and returns.

questions.q: What visibility is typical in unstable air away from showers?
c: Good, because haze is mixed upward
Poor, with haze trapped near the ground
Poor, with widespread fog at night
Poor, with persistent drizzle and stratus
questions.e: Unstable air mixes pollutants and moisture to high levels, so visibility away from precipitation is usually good.

questions.q: The ELR is 5 C per km, the SALR is 6 C per km and the DALR is 9.8 C per km. What is the stability?
questions.e: An ELR smaller than the SALR means a parcel is cooler than its environment in either state: absolutely stable.

questions.q: Compared with the dry adiabatic rate, how does the saturated adiabatic lapse rate behave in very warm, humid air?
c: It is much smaller, about 4 to 5 C per km
It is larger, above 9.8 C per km
questions.e: Latent heat released by condensation offsets cooling. In cold air the rate approaches the dry rate.

sources: Lapse rate article citing ICAO: DALR 9.8 C/km (about 3 C per 1,000 ft), SALR 3.6 to 9.2 C/km (around 5 typical), stability classes
UBC ATSC 201 course notes: DALR 9.8 C per km
Haby (theweatherprediction.com), Moist adiabatic lapse rate: varies from about 4 C/km to nearly 9.8 C/km; 4 to 5 C/km in very warm humid air; approaches the dry rate in cold air
unverified: Source is a secondary article citing ICAO, not the ICAO document itself.
Weather typical of stable and unstable air: standard teaching, not checked on a Canadian publication.
SALR direction (smaller in warm air) is now sourced to a US forecaster's page (Haby); the AMS Glossary entry gives the formula but no direction.

topics.title: Adiabatic processes and potential temperature
lesson: A process is adiabatic if no heat is exchanged with the surroundings. In the atmosphere, vertical motion is nearly adiabatic. A rising parcel meets lower pressure, expands and cools. A sinking parcel is compressed and warms.

lesson.formula:
theta = T * (1000 / p)^0.286
(T in kelvin, p in hPa)

lesson: Potential temperature (theta) is the temperature a parcel would have if brought dry adiabatically to 1000 hPa. It is conserved in dry adiabatic motion, so it labels an air parcel the way a tag labels a package.

list: Theta increasing with height: stable.
Theta constant with height: neutral (well-mixed layer).
Theta decreasing with height: unstable.

lesson: The LCL is the height where a lifted parcel becomes saturated and cloud base forms. A quick estimate:

lesson.formula: LCL height (m) = 125 * (T - Td)   [T and Td in C]

lesson: Example: T = 20 C, Td = 12 C gives about 125 x 8 = 1,000 m.

Air forced over a mountain cools at the dry rate until saturated, then at the slower moist rate while rain falls out on the windward side. Descending the lee side it warms at the full dry rate. At the same height, the lee side ends up warmer and drier. The Chinook is a Canadian example. The Canadian Encyclopedia puts the chinook belt almost entirely in southern and central Alberta, with lee-side relative humidity sometimes down to 25% or less. Part of a chinook's warmth also comes from cold Arctic air being replaced by milder maritime air.

lesson.note: Remember: lifting cools, sinking warms. Condensation slows the cooling but never the warming on the way down.

terms: Adiabatic
Without heat exchange with the surroundings.
Potential temperature
Temperature a parcel would have if moved dry adiabatically to 1000 hPa.
LCL
Lifting condensation level: height at which a lifted parcel saturates.
Foehn
Warm, dry downslope wind caused by adiabatic warming on the lee side of a mountain.

questions.q: Why does a rising, unsaturated air parcel cool?
c: It loses heat to the ground
questions.e: Lower pressure aloft lets the parcel expand. Expansion does work and lowers the temperature without heat exchange.

questions.q: For which kind of motion is potential temperature conserved?
questions.e: Potential temperature stays constant for dry adiabatic processes. Condensation adds heat and changes it.

questions.q: Surface temperature is 20 C and dew point is 12 C. Estimate the cloud base from lifting.
questions.e: LCL is about 125 m per C of spread: 125 x 8 = 1,000 m.

questions.q: What does potential temperature increasing with height indicate?
questions.e: When theta increases with height, a displaced parcel is pushed back toward its original level: stable.

questions.q: Compared with the windward side at the same height, the lee side of a mountain range during foehn is:
questions.e: Moisture is lost as precipitation on the windward side, and the descending air warms at the faster dry rate.

questions.q: Surface temperature is 25 C and dew point is 13 C. Estimate the lifting condensation level.
questions.e: LCL is about 125 x (T - Td) = 125 x 12 = 1,500 m.

questions.q: Why does a descending air parcel warm?
c: It is compressed as pressure increases
It absorbs heat from the ground
It mixes with warmer air at the same level
questions.e: Sinking air meets higher pressure and is compressed, which warms it adiabatically.

questions.q: Which description fits an adiabatic process?
c: No heat is exchanged with the surroundings
questions.e: Adiabatic means no heat exchange with the surroundings.

questions.q: Potential temperature is constant with height through a layer. What is the layer's stability?
questions.e: Constant theta means neutral stability, as in a well-mixed afternoon boundary layer.

questions.q: A saturated parcel and a dry parcel are lifted the same distance. How do their temperature changes compare?
c: The saturated parcel cools less because of latent heat
The saturated parcel cools more because condensation absorbs heat
They cool at exactly the same rate
The saturated parcel warms because of condensation
questions.e: Condensation releases latent heat, so the saturated parcel cools at the smaller moist adiabatic rate.

questions.q: Why is the lee side of a mountain warmer during a foehn?
c: Latent heat added on the windward side, then dry warming on descent
Solar heating of the lee slopes, which are bare of cloud all day
Friction between the strong wind and the rough lee slope surface
Cold air drains away from the summit and is replaced by warm air
questions.e: The air gains heat from condensation going up and warms at the full dry rate coming down.

sources: UBC ATSC 201 course notes: DALR 9.8 C per km, potential temperature exponent Rd/Cp = 0.28571
Espy's equation (Lifting condensation level article): about 125 m per C of spread, accurate to about 1%
The Canadian Encyclopedia, Chinook: formation, location, humidity
unverified: Potential temperature conservation and stability rules from theta: standard theory, not checked on a Canadian publication.
The LCL formula is an approximation that needs the dew point at the surface.
